lesson.title: Divide and Conquer: Simplifying Series-Parallel Networks
lesson.summary: Shows how to reduce circuits that combine series and parallel resistor groups into a single equivalent resistance by repeatedly collapsing recognizable sub-groups, then working back out to find individual currents and voltages.
lesson.body:
Most real circuits are not purely series or purely parallel, they are a combination of both, with some components sharing a single current path and others sharing a common voltage across separate branches. You already know both building blocks separately: in a series connection, components share one current and their resistances simply add, while in a parallel connection, components share one voltage and their conductances add, or equivalently, the reciprocal of the total resistance equals the sum of the reciprocals of each branch. A series parallel circuit is any network built by combining these two patterns.

The standard technique for analyzing such a network is reduction: repeatedly find a small group of resistors that form a clean series or parallel sub combination, collapse that group into a single equivalent resistor, redraw the simplified circuit, and repeat. Eventually the entire network reduces to one single equivalent resistance connected directly across the source. This step by step simplification lets you apply the same Ohm's law reasoning you already trust for simple series circuits, just applied one layer of complexity at a time instead of all at once.

Consider a 100 ohm resistor, R1, in series with a parallel combination of R2 at 200 ohms and R3 at 200 ohms, all connected across a 10 volt source. Start with the innermost group: R2 and R3 in parallel combine as 1 / R_parallel = 1/200 + 1/200 = 2/200, giving R_parallel = 100 ohms. Now the circuit has reduced to R1 in series with this 100 ohm equivalent, so R_total = 100 + 100 = 200 ohms. The total current from the source is I = V / R_total = 10 / 200 = 0.05 amps, or 50 milliamps, and this full 50 milliamps flows through R1 since it sits alone in the series path. That current then splits evenly between R2 and R3, because they are equal resistors in parallel, so each carries 25 milliamps, and each also has the same voltage across it, equal to I times R_parallel, or 0.05 times 100, which is 5 volts.

Notice the two step logic in that example: reduction works forward, from the full network down to a single equivalent resistance, so you can find the total current the source supplies, but then you must work backward, from that total current, through each reduction step in reverse, to recover the individual branch currents and voltages you actually care about. Skipping the backward pass is a common beginner mistake, since finding total resistance alone tells you nothing about how current splits between R2 and R3 internally.

With practice, recognizing series and parallel sub groups becomes almost automatic, and this reduction technique remains useful even for larger networks with many more resistors, as long as the network can be built up from nested series and parallel groups. Networks that cannot be reduced this way, because no two elements are purely in series or purely in parallel with each other, require more general tools like nodal analysis, which builds directly on the node concept covered at the end of this chapter.
